Hardness can be hard for noir or medium for drama. Color follows the key source.

Combine with a low fill so the near eye does not die unless you want it to. Prompt: Short lighting on [Subject], the side turned away from camera is keyed, the near side falls toward shadow, slimming and dramatic.
when: Use it to sculpt a face and put mystery on the camera side, a close-up in an office or a night bar. Do not use it when the character is presenting themselves to the public in a broad, open way.
vs: Broad lighting keys the camera-facing cheek, the reverse. Rembrandt lighting is a triangle pattern often shot short, but Rembrandt can be broad if the triangle is on the near cheek.
Split lighting is a 90-degree cut that is usually short if the dark half faces us. Side lighting describes direction, not which cheek is near camera.
examples_film: Portrait noir and Godfather-adjacent close-ups often key the far cheek so the camera sits with the shadow. Road to Perdition does the same sculpting in dark interiors.
Read the near cheek: if it is the dark one, you are short.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is broad lighting or a frontal butterfly . The tell is a bright near cheek filling the frame.
Fix it by turning the face or swinging the key onto the far side.

faq.q: What is short lighting in film?
faq.a: Lighting the side of the face turned away from camera so the near, camera-facing cheek falls toward shadow. It slims and adds dimension.

faq.q: Short lighting vs broad lighting
faq.a: Short keys the far cheek; the camera sees more shadow. Broad keys the near cheek; the camera sees more light.

faq.q: When should I use short lighting?
faq.a: Use it to sculpt a face and keep mystery on the camera side. Skip it for open, public, comic portraits.

faq.q: How do I prompt short lighting for AI image or video?
faq.a: State that the side turned away from camera is keyed and the near cheek falls toward shadow. Mention a slimming, dimensional face.

title: Side Lighting
narrative: A face or a landscape becomes sculpture. Sweat, wood grain, and cheekbones show because the light rakes.
Action and crime use it so bodies have planes; portraits use it when character should look carved. It is the wrong tool for a passport-readable hero or a beauty wrap.
Side lighting a room is not automatically split lighting . Split is the facial center-line cut with almost no wrap.
Side can still graze a shoulder, a horse, a wall.
how: Place the key at about 90 degrees, at a height that fits the story (eye height for a face, raking low sun for ground texture). Hardness is often hard so texture reads; soft side light exists as a large window in a side wall.
Color follows that source. Control wrap with flags if you need a truer split.
Prompt: Pure side light at 90 degrees on [Subject], half the face brilliant, half gone, texture and duality.
when: Use it to carve a face or a body like sculpture, a raking desert, a sweat-lit fight. Do not use it as default coverage on a two-shot that needs both people open.
vs: Split lighting is the hard facial version of this direction. Cross lighting uses two opposing side keys.
Kicker is a side-back accent, not a key. Short lighting and broad lighting depend on head turn relative to camera, not on 90 degrees as such.
examples_film: Apocalypse Now rakes faces with hard side sources in the dark. Sicario uses raking sun and side keys so landscape and faces have grain.
The job is the 90-degree rake, not a mood.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Rembrandt (too frontal) or cross lighting (a second key). The tell is a cheek triangle, or rims on both sides.
Fix it by parking one key at 90 and killing the opposite unit.

faq.q: What is side lighting in film?
faq.a: Light from about 90 degrees that emphasizes shape and texture. One side of the subject is bright; the other falls away.

faq.q: Side lighting vs split lighting
faq.a: Side lighting is the direction, usable on faces, bodies, and rooms. Split lighting is a facial pattern with a hard vertical cut and almost no wrap.

faq.q: When should I use side lighting?
faq.a: Use it to carve texture and duality. Skip it when both eyes must be openly keyed for a public conversation.

faq.q: How do I prompt side lighting for AI image or video?
faq.a: Place a single key at 90 degrees. State half the form brilliant, half gone, and name hard or soft. No second key on the far side.

title: Silhouette
narrative: Identity is less important than emblem: a rider on a ridge, a bicycle against a moon, a man in a doorway. The audience recognizes an action from outline alone.
If two shapes merge, the sentence is lost. It is the wrong tool when a line of dialogue needs a mouth, or when you still want pores and color in the coat.
A little rim is not a silhouette. If you can name the eye color, you overexposed the figure.
how: Expose for the bright ground (sky, doorway, fire, sun disk). Keep the key off the subject, or far below the background.
Backlight may exist as a sky, not as a facial key. Separate limbs, hats, and props so the outline parses.

Hardness of the background source can be hard sun or a bright overcast; the subject is simply underexposed. Prompt: Silhouette of [Subject] as a dark shape against a bright ground, surface detail gone, mythic outline only.
when: Use it when identity matters less than shape, a departure through a door, a figure against dusk. Do not use it if the action cannot be read from the outline.
vs: Backlight can create a silhouette if you expose for it, or a rim if you hold the face a little. Rim light keeps a thread of flesh highlight; silhouette usually does not.
Cameo lighting is the inverse: a lit figure on a black ground. Low-key lighting still models something in the pool.
examples_film: T. the Extra-Terrestrial puts bicycle and riders in silhouette across the moon.
The Searchers isolates a figure against a bright doorway and landscape. Lawrence of Arabia and Skyfall use desert and sun as the bright field that turns bodies into emblems.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a rim portrait or a muddy underexposure on a dark ground. The tell is visible eyes, or a black figure on a black field.
Fix it by brightening the background, killing keys on the body, and separating the limbs.

faq.q: What is a silhouette in film?
faq.a: A subject placed dark against a brighter background so contour and gesture read instead of facial detail.

faq.q: Silhouette vs rim light
faq.a: A silhouette is an unmodeled dark shape on a bright field. Rim light keeps a thin highlight on the edge of a still-dark figure, often on a dark field.

faq.q: When should I use a silhouette?
faq.a: Use it when the outline is the sentence: departure, arrival, emblem. Skip it when the face must speak.

faq.q: How do I prompt a silhouette for AI image or video?
faq.a: Ask for a dark shape against a bright ground, no surface detail, limbs separated. Expose for the sky or doorway, not the face.

title: Soft Light
narrative: Kindness, memory, overcast, a north window: the key still has a side, but the nose shadow is a gradient. Skin holds, rooms feel breathable.
You can still have contrast if the fill is low; softness is not high-key. It is the wrong tool for a gobo of blinds, a noon duel, or a split that needs a knife edge.
If the source becomes so large it surrounds the subject, direction dies and you have ambient soup.
how: Make the last surface before the subject large: silk, book light, overcast sky, big window, bounce wall. Closer and larger is softer.
Color is often daylight 5600K through diffusion, or tungsten through a large shade. Keep a key side.
Prompt: Soft wrapping light on [Subject] from a large source, gentle shadow transitions, luminous skin, north-window daylight.
when: Use it for beauty, memory, or kindness, a daylight interior, a close-up that should not cut pores into craters. Do not use it when you need projected pattern or interrogation.
vs: Hard light is the opposite quality. Bounce light is a method of getting soft.
Window light is often large and soft by architecture. Glam uses soft keys plus diffusion and catchlights.
High-key lighting uses soft sources and a lot of fill; you can have soft low-key if the wrap is large but isolated.
examples_film: The Tree of Life and Call Me by Your Name let large daylight sources wrap skin and rooms. The softness is the size of sky and window, not a beauty filter named glow.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is hard light or directionless ambient. The tell is razor edges, or no key side at all.
Fix it by enlarging the source and keeping it on one side of the face.

faq.q: What is soft light in film?
faq.a: Light from a large apparent source that wraps the subject and makes shadow edges gradual. Texture is reduced; direction can still exist.

faq.q: Soft light vs bounce light
faq.a: Soft describes the quality. Bounce is one way to create it, by reflecting off a large surface. A silk in line with the lamp is another way.

faq.q: When should I use soft light?
faq.a: Use it for kindness, memory, and most daylight interiors. Skip it when you need graphic shadow or a sharp gobo.

faq.q: How do I prompt soft light for AI image or video?
faq.a: Specify a large source, wrapping light, gentle shadow transitions. Name a window or silk on one side so direction remains.

title: Split Lighting
narrative: Duality made as geometry: hero and liar, cop and crook, the same person cut in two. The audience gets one eye in light and one in almost nothing.
Music, crime, and moral argument use it because the cut is literal. It is the wrong tool for charm, romance, or any beat that needs both cheeks.
If you sneak fill across the center line, the split collapses into side lighting with wrap. If you raise the key and pull it forward, you may accidentally make Rembrandt .
how: Put a relatively hard key at 90 degrees to the face, at about eye height, so the shadow edge runs down forehead, nose, and chin. Fill is near zero.
Color can be a hard white or a theatrical gel; the point is the cut, not prettiness. A true split is more severe than generic side light because the wrap over the nose is killed with flags if needed.
Prompt: Split lighting on [Subject], one half of the face in light, the other in shadow, a vertical moral cut.
when: Use it when a character is two things at once, a drummer under a side spot, a don in profile thought. Do not use it on a first-date close-up unless you want threat.
vs: Side lighting is the broader 90-degree direction and can still wrap a body or a room. Split is the facial pattern with a hard center line.
Rembrandt lighting keeps a triangle on the dark cheek; split does not. Loop lighting is much more frontal.
Short lighting can include a split if the dark cheek faces camera, but short is about which cheek the camera sees, not the 90-degree cut. Butterfly is the opposite: both cheeks open.
examples_film: The Godfather uses half-lit faces in the office so thought reads as a cut. Whiplash slashes players with hard side spots that often split the face on stage.
The pattern is the center line, not a mood word.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Rembrandt or wrapped side lighting . The tell is a pocket of light on the dark cheek, or a soft wrap over the nose.
Fix it by moving the key to 90 degrees and killing fill until the center line is clean.

faq.q: What is split lighting in film?
faq.a: A key at about 90 degrees that lights one half of the face and leaves the other in shadow. The cut runs vertically down the center of the face.

faq.q: Split lighting vs Rembrandt lighting
faq.a: Split has no triangle on the dark cheek; that half is gone. Rembrandt keeps a small triangle of light under the shadow-side eye.

faq.q: When should I use split lighting?
faq.a: Use it for duality, interrogation, or a theatrical side spot. Skip it when both eyes and both cheeks must sell a line.

faq.q: How do I prompt split lighting for AI image or video?
faq.a: Place the key at 90 degrees. State one half of the face in light, the other in shadow, no fill, no Rembrandt triangle.

title: Spotlight
narrative: The stage is a circle of light. A drummer, a speaker, a dancer: the instrument has a beam you can see the edge of, and stepping out of it is stepping out of the scene.
Theatre and concert coverage use it because the world really is that lamp. It is the wrong tool for a motivated apartment, or for a soft cameo with no circle.
If the pool has no edge, you have a general key in a dark room. If the figure is isolated but the source is a large silk, that is cameo , not a spot.
how: Use a focused fixture (ellipsoidal, follow spot, PAR with a tight lens) with shutters or an iris so the pool has a hard edge. Place it high and frontal or high and slightly front-side, the theatrical default.
Hardness is hard; falloff at the circle is sudden. Color is often white or a theatrical gel.
The surround is unlit. Prompt: Spotlight on [Subject], a hard pool, theater darkness around, the person as an act.
when: Use it when the stage is a circle of light, a solo, a speech, a club act. Do not use it as the key in a kitchen that has no such instrument.
vs: Cameo lighting is isolation; a spotlight is one hard instrument that can create that isolation with a visible circle. Hard light is the quality.
Top light may come from above without a circular shuttered pool. Cross lighting is two concert keys, not necessarily irised spots.
Epiphany is a story-timed change, which a spotlight snap can serve.
examples_film: Whiplash puts players in hard stage pools. Birdman 's theatre scenes treat follow spots and stage lamps as the world of the act.
The edge of the circle is the set line.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a soft cameo or a general hard key. The tell is no circle, or wrap that lights the floor evenly.
Fix it by irising a focused fixture and letting the edge of the pool be visible.

faq.q: What is a spotlight in film?
faq.a: A focused, hard-edged pool from a theatrical or similar instrument, with darkness around. The subject stands in a circle of light.

faq.q: Spotlight vs cameo lighting
faq.a: A spotlight is the instrument and its hard pool. Cameo is the result of isolating a modeled figure on black, which can also be done with a softer key and no visible circle.

faq.q: When should I use a spotlight?
faq.a: Use it for stage, concert, and any beat where stepping out of the circle leaves the scene. Skip it in ordinary rooms with no such lamp.

faq.q: How do I prompt a spotlight for AI image or video?
faq.a: Specify a hard pool, theater darkness around, a visible circular or shuttered edge. The person is an act. No soft wrap on the floor.

title: Three-Point Lighting
narrative: In a scene it is the default portrait grammar: the audience can read both eyes, the cheekbones have a light side and a shadow side, and the hair does not melt into the wall. Classical coverage uses it so reverse shots match, and so a close-up still feels like the same room as the master.
It is the wrong tool when the room already has a single honest source, or when the story wants a face half-erased. Teaching the setup is useful.
Leaving it on every night interior as three hidden movie lights is how a crime scene starts to look like a cosmetics ad.
how: Place the key about 45 degrees off camera axis and 30 to 45 degrees above the eyes, large enough to be slightly soft unless the scene is harsh. 5 to 3 stops down so the shadow cheek still has pores.

Put backlight high and behind, often slightly opposite the key, warm or white, flagged so it rims hair and shoulders without flaring the lens. Prompt: Classic three-point lighting on [Subject]: key at 45 degrees, soft fill opening shadows, warm backlight rim, modeled volume.
when: Use it for a teachable talking-head or a studio close-up that must stay readable across a whole scene. Do not use it as the only language of a night interior that is supposed to be one lamp.
vs: Key light is the dominant source inside this setup, not the setup itself. Fill light only opens the key's shadows; it has no third direction.
Backlight is the rear unit that separates the figure. Rembrandt lighting and loop lighting are facial patterns you can make with the key while the other two points still exist.
examples_film: Casablanca and Rebecca show the classical Hollywood version: key, fill, and a hair or back edge kept in ratio so stars stay modeled in every size. Use that grammar, not a poster to copy.
Later films keep the three jobs even when the units are hidden in practicals.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a single frontal soft light labeled as three-point. The tell is even cheeks, no hair edge, and a shadowless nose.
Fix it by offsetting the key, dropping fill, and adding a flagged rear rim.

faq.q: What is three-point lighting in film?
faq.a: A conventional arrangement of key, fill, and backlight. The key sets direction and exposure, fill opens the shadow side, and backlight separates the subject from the background.

faq.q: Three-point lighting vs key light
faq.a: Key light is one source. Three-point lighting is a three-job system in which that key is joined by a dimmer fill and a rear separation light.

faq.q: When should I use three-point lighting?
faq.a: Use it when a face must stay fully readable and consistent across coverage. Skip it when a single motivated source should own the room.

faq.q: How do I prompt three-point lighting for AI image or video?
faq.a: State key at about 45 degrees, soft fill on the opposite cheek, and a warm or white backlight rim. Name which side is keyed so the model does not flatten the face.

title: Top Light
narrative: Power sitting in a chair, or guilt: the head is a skull with a lid of light. Crime bosses, interrogations, and some night exteriors use overhead so the eyes recede.
The person is still human; the pupils must not emit. It is the wrong tool for glamour.
If you bring the source forward of the head you get butterfly . If you need a catchlight, add a tiny eye light rather than lowering the overhead until it becomes a frontal key.
how: Hang a lamp or use a ceiling practical directly above, flagged so it does not rake the nose as a frontal. Hardness can be hard (bare bulb) for a skull, or a bit softer (shaded pendant) for a diner.
Color is often tungsten, sometimes cool industrial. Keep exposure on the forehead, not in the sockets, unless you add a separate eye glint.
Prompt: A lamp directly above [Subject], light falling on forehead and shoulders, eye sockets in shadow, human eyes, no light emitting from the pupils.
when: Use it for a figure of power in a chair, a diner pendant, a guilty face under a garage bulb. Do not use it as beauty lighting.
vs: Underlighting is the opposite direction, from below. Butterfly lighting is high but still in front of the face.
Low-key lighting is the ratio that often houses top light. Hair light is behind and above, not a downward key on the forehead.
Cameo may use a top pool but is about isolating the figure in void.
examples_film: The Godfather is the famous overhead office: forehead and hands, eyes in wells. The Batman (2022) uses overhead rain and practicals so faces sit under lids of light.
The sockets stay dark on purpose.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is butterfly or glowing eyes. The tell is an under-nose butterfly with open sockets, or pupils that shine like LEDs.
Fix it by moving the source truly overhead and keeping eyes as dark human surfaces with at most a tiny catch.

faq.q: What is top light in film?
faq.a: Light from directly above that hits forehead and shoulders and drops the eye sockets into shadow. It is a downward key, not a hair rim.

faq.q: Top light vs butterfly lighting
faq.a: Butterfly is high and in front, opening both eyes with a small nose shadow. Top light is overhead enough that the sockets hollow.

faq.q: When should I use top light?
faq.a: Use it for power, guilt, a pendant over a table, a boss in a chair. Skip it for glamour.

faq.q: How do I prompt top light for AI image or video?
faq.a: Place a lamp directly above. Light on forehead and shoulders, eye sockets in shadow, human eyes, no light from the pupils.

title: Underlighting
narrative: The source is fire, a screen on the floor, a flashlight under a chin, or a monster. Faces invert: the brow ridge goes dark, the nostrils and chin light up.
Horror and campfire talk use the same physics; only the object changes. It is the wrong tool for ordinary conversation under a ceiling.
A candle on a table can underlight if it sits below the chin, but candlelight is a source type that can also sit beside a face. Underlighting is the direction.
how: Place a lamp, flame, or panel below the chin, pointing up. Keep it close so inverse-square falloff hits the face and dies on the ceiling.
Hardness is often hard or small-soft (a phone screen is a smallish source). Color is flame-warm, screen-cool, or theatrical green; the climb of the shadows is the tell.
Prompt: A lamp on the table below [Subject]'s chin, pointing up. Shadows climb the cheekbones and eye sockets.
The source is under the face, not beside it.
when: Use it when the source is fire, a floor screen, or a threat under the chin. Do not use it as a default beauty fill from a white card unless you want unease.
vs: Top light is the opposite. Candlelight may underlight if the flame is low, but a candelabra at face height is more of a small frontal or side key.
Practical lighting is the visible object; underlighting is where it sits. Glam sometimes uses a weak under fill (a reflector) that must stay far below key so it does not invert the face.
examples_film: James Whale's Frankenstein (1931) underlights the creature so the brow and sockets invert. Hereditary uses low sources and ritual light to the same uncanny effect.
The shadows must climb, not slide sideways.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is side lighting or a candle off to the side. The tell is a left-right split instead of shadows that climb.
Fix it by lowering the source below the jaw and aiming up.

faq.q: What is underlighting in film?
faq.a: Lighting from below the face so shadows climb the cheeks and sockets. It inverts ordinary daylight modeling and often feels uncanny.

faq.q: Underlighting vs top light
faq.a: Top light comes from above and hollows the eyes from overhead. Underlighting comes from below and lights the chin and nostrils while the brow goes dark.

faq.q: When should I use underlighting?
faq.a: Use it for firelight below the face, a screen on the floor, or a horror invert. Skip it for ordinary daylight talk.

faq.q: How do I prompt underlighting for AI image or video?
faq.a: Place the lamp or flame under the chin, pointing up. State that shadows climb the cheekbones and sockets, source under the face, not beside it.

title: Volumetric Light
narrative: Air has to be photographed. A cathedral, a forest, a smoky archive: the beam is architecture.
The source implies a world outside the frame. Without particles you only see where the light lands, not the path it took.
It is the wrong tool in clean air if you still want shafts, or when haze is so thick that every depth plane flattens. Disconnected glowing stripes with no lamp are not volumetric light.
They are stickers.
how: You need a directional source (often hard, slightly back or high) and a scattering medium: haze, dust, rain, smoke. The camera usually sees some of the beam angle, which is why backlight helps.
Color follows the source: warm sun, cool window, searchlight white. Limit haze so foreground and background still separate.
Prompt: Volumetric rays through haze around [Subject], visible beams, dust in the shaft, cathedral or forest light as architecture.
when: Use it when the air is part of the picture, a smoky interior, a forest morning, a searchlight. Do not add floating stripes with no source and no medium.
vs: Backlight is the direction that often reveals volume. Atmospheric haze is the medium.
Dappled light patterns surfaces; volume patterns the air. Epiphany may use a sudden shaft, but epiphany is a change timed to understanding.
Silhouette can sit inside a bright shaft if the figure stays dark.
examples_film: Blade Runner 2049 builds interiors where dust and haze make shafts physical. The Tree of Life lets forest and interior sun become visible architecture.
Blade Runner (1982) searchlights through smoke are the same physics.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a backlight rim with no air, or painted god-ray stickers. The tell is stripes that ignore the lamp and the body.
Fix it by adding a scattering medium and a real rear or high source, then letting the body interrupt the beam.

faq.q: What is volumetric light in film?
faq.a: Beams made visible by haze, fog, dust, smoke, or particles. You photograph the path of the light, not only where it lands.

faq.q: Volumetric light vs backlight
faq.a: Backlight is the direction from behind. Volumetric light is the beam made visible in a medium. Backlight often helps you see that beam.

faq.q: When should I use volumetric light?
faq.a: Use it when air, dust, or smoke should be visible architecture. Skip it in clean air, or when haze would flatten every plane.

faq.q: How do I prompt volumetric light for AI image or video?
faq.a: Specify a real source and a scattering medium, visible beams, dust in the shaft. The body can interrupt the beam. No orphan glowing stripes.

title: Window Light
narrative: Day interiors without looking lit. A figure sits in the falloff, one side toward glass, the far wall dying.

Painterly rooms, period houses, and quiet dramas use the window as the only key so the hour is readable. It is the wrong tool at night (unless moonlight through glass is the story), or when you need a hard bulb.
A window is not automatically bounce ; bounce happens after the light hits a wall. A window can be hard if the sun is direct and small in the frame of the glass.
how: Use real sky or a large source outside the glass, plus sheers if you want wrap. Direction is the window's side.
Hardness: overcast or north light is soft; direct sun through dirty glass is harder and may throw a patch. Color is daylight, cooler if north sky, warmer late.
Let inverse-square and flags create falloff toward the room. Prompt: Window light as the only key on [Subject], large soft directional source, falloff into the room, painterly interior.
when: Use it for a day interior that should not look studio-lit, a sitting room, a workshop. Do not use a frontal silk that ignores the window's actual wall.
vs: Soft light is the usual quality of north windows. Motivated lighting is the logic that lets you hide a source outside that window.
Bounce is the wall ricochet after entry. Available light uses the real window without adding.
Golden hour through a window is a specific color and angle of this source.
examples_film: Girl with a Pearl Earring (2003) builds interiors as if Vermeer's window were the key. The Danish Girl uses large directional day interiors with falloff.
The grammar is glass, falloff, and one side, not a painting to clone.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a frontal soft key that does not match the window wall, or a hard gobo of blinds when you asked for wrap. The tell is a key from a blank wall.
Fix it by putting the bright side on the glass and letting the room fall off.

faq.q: What is window light in film?
faq.a: Light shaped as if it enters through a window: large, directional, with falloff into the room. The window is the source and the modifier.

faq.q: Window light vs bounce light
faq.a: Window light is the entry from glass and sky. Bounce is a ricochet off a surface, which a window may cause once it hits a wall, but bounce is not the window itself.

faq.q: When should I use window light?
faq.a: Use it for day interiors that should feel architectural rather than studio-lit. Skip it when the story is a night bulb.

faq.q: How do I prompt window light for AI image or video?
faq.a: State window light as the only key, large directional source, falloff into the room. Name the window wall and the sky condition.

title: Boomerang
narrative: Use it to weaponize a small motion: hair toss, splash, a jump's peak, a door that never finishes closing. Both directions must read.
If the forward pass is ugly, the reverse will not save it. Loops work when the end of the reverse meets the start of the forward without a bump.
It is the wrong tool for grief, inverted physics as story, or a seamless forward-only cycle (a pendulum designed to sew). Reverse motion one way is a spell.
An infinite loop may never reverse. Do not boomerang a line of dialogue whose words cannot run backward.
how: Record a short, readable gesture with clean contacts, play it forward, then reverse the same frames. Trim so the join is at a still-ish peak or a matched pose.
Camera usually locked. Prompt: Boomerang of [Subject], action running forward then snapping backward on the same path, a loop of coming and going.
when: Use it to turn a splash, a jump, or a hair toss into a toy loop. Do not use it for a one-way undo of a crash.
vs: A boomerang is not one-way Reverse Motion . It is not an Infinite Loop that sews last frame to first while staying forward.
A Moonwalk is a body's lie in living time. A Cinemagraph freezes most of a still and loops one element.
examples_film: Instagram and Vine made the round-trip native. Music videos use it as a hook on a single gesture.
Feature grammar rarely needs it except as a quoted phone-screen or a title-card gag.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Reverse Motion or a forward Infinite Loop . The tell is rain that only rises, or a loop that never rewinds.
Fix: specify forward then back on the same samples, and a join that matches.

faq.q: What is Boomerang in film?
faq.a: A boomerang plays a short action forward and then backward on the same path, often as a loop, so the gesture comes and goes.

faq.q: Boomerang vs Reverse Motion
faq.a: Reverse motion rewinds once and stays in that direction. A boomerang is a round trip: forward, then back, usually repeating.

faq.q: When should I use Boomerang?
faq.a: When a small physical gesture should become a toy: splash, jump, toss. Both directions must remain readable.

faq.q: How do I prompt Boomerang for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write that [Subject] plays forward then reverses along the same motion as a seamless loop. Forbid a one-way reverse and a forward-only sew.

title: Bullet Time
narrative: Use it when a split-second decision should become architecture. The audience seems to occupy a viewpoint no observer inside the event could have.
Debris, rain, and coat tails hang so we can walk around them. The path is one move, usually an arc.
It is the wrong tool for a dinner scene, a lyric walk, or a simple impact study from a locked camera. If the camera is locked, you wanted frozen in motion or a freeze.
If the fighter keeps moving at stretched rate and the camera stays put, you wanted slow motion. Do not add a zoom on top of the orbit unless you are making a different shot.
how: Use a synchronized or time-offset multi-camera array with interpolation, or a fully controlled 3D scene. Enforce frozen or near-frozen subject geometry while changing viewpoint.
Particles should be countable and rigid enough to survive the arc. Prompt: Bullet time around [Subject], the moment frozen while the camera orbits, a slice of time as a sculpture.
when: Use it to inspect an impact, a leap, or a dodge that already happened, as on a rooftop lean under gunfire. Do not use it as slow motion with a shaky camera.
vs: Bullet time is not Slow Motion , which stretches action without requiring a traveling viewpoint around a hold. It is not a normal 360-Degree Orbit , which circles living time.
It is not Freeze Frame , which stops the camera too. Frozen in Motion may let a chosen person move through a stopped world.
Bullet time stops or crushes the event while the camera walks around it.
examples_film: The Matrix rooftop, Neo leaning under gunfire, is the textbook array move. Wanted curves bullets as inspectable paths through space.
Later action films borrow the split between body-time and camera-time. Prompt the physics, not a trademark.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is handheld Slow Motion . The tell is a moving fighter and a camera that does not orbit, or a freeze with no parallax.
Fix: subject frozen or nearly frozen, camera orbits a named arc, debris hanging, consistent shadows.

faq.q: What is Bullet Time in film?
faq.a: Bullet time is a viewpoint traveling around an event that is frozen or radically slowed, so camera speed and subject time are no longer the same clock.

faq.q: Bullet Time vs Slow Motion
faq.a: Slow motion stretches the action. Bullet time nearly stops the action and moves the camera around it, often with an array or a 3D reconstruction.

faq.q: When should I use Bullet Time?
faq.a: When a split-second must be inspected as space: a dodge, a leap, an impact the audience should walk around.

faq.q: How do I prompt Bullet Time for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write that time freezes around [Subject] while the camera orbits. Demand hanging debris and frozen geometry. Ban ordinary slow motion and lock-off stills.

title: Fast Motion
narrative: Use it when real time cannot hold the life in front of the lens: a factory that never stops, a city that should feel over-efficient, a chase whose danger is relentlessness rather than one punch. Subtle acceleration can be funnier or more oppressive than a cartoon speed-up.
Keep sound on its own clock. Pitch-shifted footsteps often betray the trick.
It is the wrong tool for weather, construction, or a night becoming morning. Those need interval sampling, not sped-up continuous action.
If the camera itself steps through space while hours collapse, you wanted a hyperlapse. Do not accelerate a performance whose contacts and gravity must stay honest.
how: Undercrank (shoot fewer frames per second than playback) or retime in the cut with a planned speed ratio. Longer exposure per frame, if the shutter stays open, increases motion blur.
Check hands, object contacts, and foot cadence after the speed change. Prompt: Undercranked fast motion of [Subject], crowds smearing, clouds racing, planned speed ratio, coherent contacts.
when: Use it when a mailroom, assembly line, or crowd must feel over-efficient, as in a comic or cosmic crush of ordinary work. Do not use it to stand in for a day-to-night sky.
vs: Fast motion speeds continuous action. Time-Lapse samples the world at long intervals so slow change (shadows, crowds as systems) plays quickly.
Hyperlapse is time-lapse plus a camera that advances through space. Slow Motion is the inverse stretch.
A Speed Ramp changes rate inside one shot rather than holding a constant acceleration.
examples_film: Modern Times uses factory rhythm so mechanized work feels like a speeded machine wearing a man. A Clockwork Orange undercranks selected passages so appetite and violence become brisk, grotesque efficiency.
Mad Max: Fury Road alters cadence on chosen action beats rather than running the whole film as a cartoon. Koyaanisqatsi is often grouped here, but its urban crush is mostly interval time-lapse.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Time-Lapse . The tell is a racing crowd under a sun and shadows that never move, or people who teleport instead of stepping.
Fix: keep continuous action and a planned speed ratio, then check contacts. If hours must collapse, change to interval photography.

faq.q: What is Fast Motion in film?
faq.a: Fast motion is undercranked or retimed action that occupies less screen time than it took in the world, so movement looks accelerated.

faq.q: Fast Motion vs Time-Lapse
faq.a: Fast motion speeds a continuous take. Time-lapse captures frames at long intervals so processes too slow for real time (light, weather, crowds as flow) play in seconds.

faq.q: When should I use Fast Motion?
faq.a: When ordinary movement should feel over-efficient, comic, or relentless, and the action itself is still a continuous performance.

faq.q: How do I prompt Fast Motion for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write undercranked or accelerated playback, crowds and weather racing, and coherent contacts. Do not ask for hours of sun travel unless you actually want time-lapse.

title: Freeze Frame
narrative: Use it when the fact is the picture itself: a boy at the edge of the sea, a narrator labeling a life, a triumph that should not continue into the next second. Grain, dust, and expression stay.

Sound may keep running (voiceover, a song, a crowd) so the freeze feels like a caption, not a crash. It is the wrong tool when you still need motion around a stopped body, or a camera that walks around an instant.
Those are frozen-in-motion and bullet time. A posed tableau with living extras is not a freeze.
Do not freeze a line of dialogue whose meaning is in the next word.
how: Select one frame and reprint or hold it for the required duration. An optical zoom into that still (as at the end of The 400 Blows ) is a move on a photograph, not new live action.
The shutter is no longer sampling. Prompt: Freeze frame on [Subject], the world stopping on a decisive pose, grain holding, a still torn out of time.
when: Use it to end, to joke, or to offer evidence, such as a final still of a runaway on a beach. Do not use it when particles should hang while the camera still travels.
vs: A freeze is not Slow Motion , which continues to sample the action, only slower. It is not Frozen in Motion , where a chosen person or the camera may still move while the world holds.
It is not Bullet Time , an orbit around a sculpture of speed. A Tableau is staged stillness inside living time, extras breathing, not a held frame.
examples_film: The 400 Blows ends on Antoine at the water, the image arrested so the boy cannot run farther. Goodfellas freezes Henry so voiceover can label a life mid-gesture.
Rocky is often cited for punctuation energy around a still of triumph. Trainspotting is listed beside freeze grammar more for its opening jolt than for a single copied hold.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Frozen in Motion or Bullet Time . The tell is rain or coat tails hanging while the viewpoint keeps traveling, or a mid-air sculpture with parallax.
Fix: stop the camera and the world on one frame. If you need a walk around the instant, change technique.

faq.q: What is Freeze Frame in film?
faq.a: A freeze frame is a held still taken from the moving picture, so story time stops on one image.

faq.q: Freeze Frame vs Frozen in Motion
faq.a: A freeze holds the entire picture, camera included. Frozen in motion stops most of the world while a chosen body or the viewpoint may continue.

faq.q: When should I use Freeze Frame?
faq.a: When the still is the point: an ending, a joke, or a face presented as evidence. Let sound carry if the hold needs a caption.

faq.q: How do I prompt Freeze Frame for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write that action freezes into one still and holds, grain included, camera stopped. Ban orbits, hanging debris, and continued footsteps.

title: Frozen in Motion
narrative: Use it to separate a mind from consequence: superhuman perception, a wish to step outside a square, a kitchen instant stretched into a walk. Julie can run through a stopped Oslo.
Quicksilver can work a room the rest of the world cannot occupy. Hair, weather, shadows, and loose objects must obey the same freeze or the illusion dies.

It is the wrong tool when the whole picture should hold (freeze-frame), when the camera should orbit a crushed event (bullet time), or when crowds should race around a statue (timelapse human). Do not freeze the hero and the street together unless you mean a still.
how: Decide the rule: extras hold, fluids and debris are suspended, the subject and/or camera may travel. Use held extras and practical supports for simple beats, VFX or 3D for complex hangs.
Prompt: Frozen-in-motion of [Subject], the world stopped mid-gesture, particles hanging, [Subject] or the camera still allowed to move.
when: Use it when one person should walk a stopped street, or work a stopped kitchen, while pigeons and extras hang. Do not use it as a freeze of the entire frame, and do not race the crowd.
vs: Frozen in motion is not Freeze Frame (camera and world both stop). It is not Bullet Time (event crushed, camera orbits a sculpture).
It is not Timelapse Human (crowd races, hero holds). Slow Motion still advances everyone, only slower.
Keep the permission list explicit.
examples_film: X-Men: Days of Future Past expands Quicksilver's Pentagon kitchen into a subjective instant the others cannot share. The Worst Person in the World lets Julie run through an Oslo whose other inhabitants are suspended.
The Matrix rooftop is the orbiting cousin, bullet time, not this split of who may walk.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Freeze Frame , Bullet Time , or Timelapse Human . The tell is a fully still picture, an orbit around a statue, or people as smoke.
Fix: write the freeze rule, hang the extras, and let only the chosen body or camera continue.

faq.q: What is Frozen in Motion in film?
faq.a: Frozen in motion stops most of the world while a chosen person and/or the camera keep moving, so one clock splits from the rest.

faq.q: Frozen in Motion vs Bullet Time
faq.a: Bullet time walks the camera around a nearly frozen event. Frozen in motion lets a character inhabit a stopped world, not only inspect it from an orbit.

faq.q: When should I use Frozen in Motion?
faq.a: When one person's experience should leave the world's clock: a run through a stopped city, a superhuman chore in a held kitchen.

faq.q: How do I prompt Frozen in Motion for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write a stopped environment, hanging particles, and a clear permission: who may move. Ban a full freeze, a racing crowd, and an array orbit unless you want those cousins.

title: Infinite Loop
narrative: As a picture machine, design a motion whose end state matches its start: position, light, pose. The cut should vanish.
As a story machine, repeat an event sequence while knowledge or one decision changes. Those are cousins that share a name.
Do not prompt them as one blob. It is the wrong tool for a forward-back toy (boomerang) or a mostly still image with one living detail (cinemagraph).
A loop that changes everything at once has no baseline. A join that flashes is just a cut.
how: For a visual loop, match the first and last frames and keep the action forward. For a narrative loop, establish a reset cue and a stable baseline, then vary a small number of actions per cycle.
Prompt: Infinite loop of [Subject], the last frame sewing to the first, a motion that never arrives.
when: Use it when a motion or a day should fail to conclude, such as a walk cycle that sews or a morning that resets. Do not use it when you want a boomerang snap.
vs: An infinite loop is not a Boomerang , which rewinds the same samples. A Cinemagraph holds a still and loops one island of motion.
Reverse Motion is direction, not a sew. Narrative loops ( Groundhog Day ) change behavior inside a repeated event.
Visual loops must match ends.
examples_film: GIF culture and installation video are the visual grammar: a motion that can play forever. Groundhog Day returns the same morning while Phil's behavior changes.
Run Lola Run repeats attempts with varied actions and outcomes. Edge of Tomorrow turns repetition into training.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Boomerang . The tell is a visible rewind, or a reset with no matching frames.
Fix: match last frame to first, keep direction consistent, and change only the variables you mean to change.

faq.q: What is Infinite Loop in film?
faq.a: An infinite loop either sews last frame to first so a motion never ends, or repeats an event sequence while knowledge or choices change.

faq.q: Infinite Loop vs Boomerang
faq.a: A boomerang runs forward then backward on the same path. A visual infinite loop usually stays forward and matches its ends so the join vanishes.

faq.q: When should I use Infinite Loop?
faq.a: When duration should not progress: a seamless cycle, or a repeated day that makes one changed decision comparable.

faq.q: How do I prompt Infinite Loop for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write a seamless loop, end matching start, no visible cut. If you mean a repeated-day story, say the reset cue and what changes each cycle.

title: Long Take
narrative: Use it when incompatible facts must coexist in one geography: boredom beside danger, a joke beside a wound, a bomb in a trunk while people chat. The eye scans a functioning world instead of consuming an insert.
Duration is the tension. A dense crowd is not enough.
Each zone needs an intelligible action timed to the camera. It is the wrong tool when the scene is a virtuoso ride that may hide joins, or when coverage should isolate a face.
A oner is designed to play as one take and may be stitched. A long take's claim is continuous time.
Do not hold a static close-up for two minutes and call the endurance a panorama.
how: Block foreground, midground, and background on a shared timeline. Give the camera a clear route (Steadicam, crane, handheld, or studio dolly) and vary its attention without losing the human anchor.
Rehearse contacts, eyelines, and extra business so the take can survive. Prompt: Long take covering [Subject] without a cut, duration as tension, blocking and camera choreographed as one sentence.
when: Use it when the audience must stay in the room, such as a car that cannot cut away from incoming gunfire. Do not use it to show off a corridor walk with nothing happening in depth.
vs: A long take emphasizes continuous duration. A Oner is designed to play without visible edits and may hide stitches.
Steadicam is a support, not a duration claim. An Invisible Cut is how some oners cheat.
A Master Shot covers the action so the scene can be cut. A long take often is the scene.
examples_film: Children of Men keeps car and birth passages inside continuous danger. The Player opens by walking conversations across a studio lot in one moving sentence.
Touch of Evil follows a bomb car while nearby people remain unaware. Atonement 's Dunkirk beach moves among soldiers, wreckage, and stranded activity.
Russian Ark and Victoria extend the wager to feature length.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a stitched Oner sold as uncut truth, or a crowded wide with no timed business. The tell is a whip into darkness, a crossing truck, or extras who only occupy space.
Fix: one overt take, distinct actions in depth, a camera route, and a human anchor.

faq.q: What is Long Take in film?
faq.a: A long take is an unusually extended shot that keeps performance, space, and duration continuous without an overt cut.

faq.q: Long Take vs Oner
faq.a: A long take claims continuous recorded time. A oner is designed to play as one take and may include invisible stitches as long as the joins do not read.

faq.q: When should I use Long Take?
faq.a: When leaving the room would leak tension, and the world in depth must keep working around the people we follow.

faq.q: How do I prompt Long Take for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write an unbroken take with no cut, a camera route, and separate actions in foreground, midground, and background. Name the human anchor.

title: Low Shutter
narrative: Use it when impact and sensory stress should feel exposed: rain as beads, limbs as chopped positions, a landing that does not silk over. You are not speeding the scene.
You are removing the blur that usually glues fragments together. Combat and panic live here.
It is the wrong tool for night-traffic ribbons, lyric smear, or silk slow motion. Photography says 'low shutter speed' for long exposure.
Film says low shutter angle for the opposite. If every lamp paints a ribbon, you shot motion blur.
Do not skip frames and call that short shutter.
how: At 24 fps, a 180-degree shutter is about 1/48 s. A 45-degree shutter is about 1/192 s: less blur, more light required.
Compensate exposure. In generated footage, request low motion blur and crisp droplets, not missing frames.
Prompt: Low-shutter (short shutter angle) of [Subject], reduced motion blur, crisp rain and limb edges, staccato cadence.
when: Use it on a landing, a rescue run, or a fight that should feel like discrete fragments, such as Omaha-style rain and bodies. Do not use it when lamps should drag as ribbons.
vs: Low shutter here is the inverse of Motion Blur . A Whip Pan smears by rotating fast, usually with a normal or long shutter.
Slow Motion can look sharp because high fps shortens each exposure, but the clock is stretched. Stutter / Stop-Stutter drops frames.
Short shutter, low frame rate, skipped frames, and speed changes are separate controls.
examples_film: Saving Private Ryan 's Omaha Beach landing is the grammar: sharp, harshly segmented movement. Gladiator uses aggressive, discontinuous-looking motion on selected battle images.
Cloverfield is listed nearby for chaos, but much of that chaos is handheld smear, the cousin.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Motion Blur (and the phrase 'low shutter speed'). The tell is ribbons of light and unreadable rain.
Fix: specify short shutter angle or 1/200 s class exposure, reduced motion blur, staccato edges. If you wanted paint, go to motion blur.

faq.q: What is Low Shutter in film?
faq.a: Low shutter here means a short shutter angle: each frame is exposed briefly, so motion stays crisp and staccato instead of smeared.

faq.q: Low Shutter vs Motion Blur
faq.a: Motion blur streaks because the shutter stays open during movement. Low shutter angle cuts that blur so fragments of action stay sharp.

faq.q: When should I use Low Shutter?
faq.a: When a hit, a run, or a landing should feel like exposed fragments at normal speed, not like silk and not like night-traffic ribbons.

faq.q: How do I prompt Low Shutter for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write short shutter angle, reduced motion blur, and crisp rain or limbs at normal playback. Do not ask for long-exposure streaks.

title: Moonwalk
narrative: Use it when gait itself is the spectacle: dance, a villain who does not obey floors, a sidewalk that should feel like ice. Wet asphalt or a stage helps the read.
Coat tails should trail the slide, not bounce like steps. It is the wrong tool for a chase on gravel, a grief undo, or a toy loop.
Reverse motion would rewind the whole world. A boomerang would come and go.
A double dolly puts subject and camera on one platform so the world slides while the walk may be ordinary. Moonwalk is the body's lie.
Do not also spin or levitate.
how: Write a backward slide, upright torso, one foot gliding, the other pushing. Camera can lock or track laterally.
Keep contact with the floor. Prompt: Moonwalk of [Subject], backward glide that reads as forward myth, slide as dance grammar.
when: Use it when the walk is the trick, such as a backward glide on wet night asphalt. Do not use it as reversed footage of an ordinary walk.
vs: A moonwalk is not Reverse Motion of a forward walk (that inverts the whole street). It is not a Boomerang loop.
A Double Dolly can fake a similar float by moving person and camera together, world sliding, feet possibly still walking. Moonwalk deletes the heel-lift.
Infinite Loop may sew a glide but is a join, not a gait.
examples_film: Moonwalker and Jackson's music videos are the grammar: the still is the middle of the glide, not a pose at rest. Later videos quote the slide.
Spike Lee's double-dolly is the camera-platform cousin, a different physical cause for a similar dream of locomotion.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is walking backward normally, or Reverse Motion . The tell is a heel lift, swinging arms of a walk, or rain rising.
Fix: flat glide, upright torso, floor contact, world still running forward.

faq.q: What is Moonwalk in film?
faq.a: A moonwalk is a backward slide performed as dance grammar: the body glides, the heel does not walk, the world keeps its forward clock.

faq.q: Moonwalk vs Double Dolly
faq.a: Double dolly moves performer and camera together so the world slides. Moonwalk is the feet lying: a glide that can be shot with a locked or laterally tracking camera.

faq.q: When should I use Moonwalk?
faq.a: When gait is the spectacle and the floor should feel like ice. Skip it on terrain that cannot sell a slide.

faq.q: How do I prompt Moonwalk for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write a backward glide, upright torso, one foot sliding, heel not lifting. Keep the world running forward. Ban reverse footage and levitation.

title: Motion Blur
narrative: Use it when speed or trauma should smear: headlights as ribbons, a body that cannot be counted, a whip that erases geography for a frame. Normal 180-degree film already has some blur.
This look commits further, so edges fail on purpose. It is the wrong tool for staccato combat that should feel like discrete fragments.
That is short shutter, often misfiled under the same war films. Slow motion with dense samples can look sharper, not smearier.
Do not add a blur overlay on a sharp take and call it shutter.
how: Expose long enough, or move fast enough, that edges streak within the frame. A Whip Pan is a burst of this.
A locked camera with a racing subject is the other axis. Night lamps help because they write ribbons.
Prompt: Long-shutter motion blur on [Subject] or the world, streaks of light, bodies smearing.
when: Use it when a night street or a panicked camera move should smear, such as lamps dragging during a run. Do not use it when you want Saving Private Ryan 's crisp, segmented droplets.
vs: Motion blur is smear from exposure. Low Shutter in this library is short shutter: reduced blur, staccato edges.
A Whip Pan is camera rotation fast enough to erase the middle. Slow Motion often looks sharper because each high-fps frame is a shorter exposure.
Step Printing smears and steps. Do not confuse photography's 'low shutter speed' with film's low shutter angle.
examples_film: Cloverfield lets handheld panic smear the monster and the street. Whip-heavy action (the Bourne films among them) uses bursts of blur as geography fails.
Saving Private Ryan is often listed here, but Omaha Beach is largely short-shutter staccato, the cousin, not the smear.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Low Shutter (short shutter angle). The tell is crispy rain and chopped limbs with no ribbons.
Fix: drag the shutter or increase motion until lights streak. If you wanted SPR cadence, change technique rather than adding a blur filter.

faq.q: What is Motion Blur in film?
faq.a: Motion blur is streaking or softness from subject or camera movement while the shutter is open. It is exposure plus velocity, not a separate object.

faq.q: Motion Blur vs Low Shutter
faq.a: Motion blur is smear from a longer exposure relative to movement. Low shutter here means a short shutter angle: sharper, staccato frames with less blur.

faq.q: When should I use Motion Blur?
faq.a: When speed or trauma should paint: night lamps as ribbons, a whip that erases the middle, a body that cannot be counted.

faq.q: How do I prompt Motion Blur for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write long-shutter streaks, dragging lights, and smearing bodies. Demand that raindrops and limbs are not all crisp.

title: Oner
narrative: Use it when geography, breath, and choreography should feel like one continuous push: a backstage spiral, a trench, an extraction through apartments. Hidden cuts are allowed only if they are invisible.
The audience should not be able to point to the splice. The camera and the blocking are one machine.
It is the wrong tool when the ethical claim is uncut duration, or when the scene is a quiet two-person talk that only needs a master. A true long take refuses the stitch.
A oner may use it. Do not call three coverage angles a oner because the editor was smooth.
how: Choreograph a path that can be performed, then decide where a join could hide if the take cannot be true. Steadicam, crane, and handheld all work if the breath stays consistent.
Match lighting and eyelines across stitches. Prompt: Apparent oner of [Subject], a whole scene as one take, hidden cuts allowed only if invisible.
when: Use it when the scene is a ride through connected actions, such as a backstage spiral or a trench crossing. Do not use it for a static conversation that only needs coverage.
vs: A Long Take emphasizes uncut duration as a fact. A oner emphasizes the ride and may be stitched.
Steadicam is often the support. An Invisible Cut is the join.
Tracking Shot and Follow Shot can exist inside a oner without making every track a oner.
examples_film: Birdman plays backstage panic as one apparent breath, stitches hidden. 1917 connects trench and field into a continuous war path, also stitched.
Extraction runs apartment and vehicle action as a designed single-take sequence. Compare those with Russian Ark , a true feature-length take, if the claim is uncut fact rather than ride.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is ordinary coverage, or a Long Take you secretly cut. The tell is a change of breath, a jump in extra positions, or a whip that does not match.
Fix: one visible path, matched energy across any hidden join, and no insert that admits the splice.

faq.q: What is Oner in film?
faq.a: A oner is a shot designed to play without visible edits, whether it is a true single take or a stitched sequence whose joins do not read.

faq.q: Oner vs Long Take
faq.a: A long take is continuous recorded duration. A oner is the ride: it can be true or stitched, as long as the audience cannot see the cut.

faq.q: When should I use Oner?
faq.a: When the scene should feel like one breath through connected spaces and actions, and coverage would leak the charge.

faq.q: How do I prompt Oner for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write a continuous oner following [Subject] through connected actions with no visible cut. Name the path. Allow hidden cuts only if they stay invisible.

title: Reverse Motion
narrative: Use it for trick photography, grief that wants an undo, or a world whose physics run the other way. The audience reads inverted inertia: water, cloth, sparks, and footsteps all lie.
A single reversed gesture can feel like a spell. A whole reversed fight can feel like entropy running downhill in the wrong direction.
It is the wrong tool when you only need a toy loop, or when the plot itself is told from consequence to cause without reversing the footage. A boomerang goes forward then back on the same path.
Memento -style chronology reorders scenes at normal playback. Do not mix those machines in one prompt.
how: Shoot the action forward with readable contacts, then reverse the clip. Gravity , fluids, and cloth are the proof.

A person putting on a coat forward will look like an impossible undressing in reverse only if the fabric was honest on the way in. Prompt: Reverse motion of [Subject], time running backward, rain rising, a broken thing assembling.
when: Use it when a broken object should reassemble, or rain should rise, as a visible undo. Do not use it to mean reverse story order with ordinary-speed scenes.
vs: Reverse playback is not reverse chronology. Boomerang runs the same action forward then back as a loop.
Slow Motion only changes rate, not direction. An Infinite Loop sews last frame to first and may stay forward.
Tenet mixes inverted world-lines with true reversed footage. Memento and Irréversible mostly reorder scenes.
examples_film: Tenet lets objects and people move through events against the local clock, including true reversed photography. Cocteau's Orphée and related trick shots reverse ordinary gestures so they read as rites.

Memento opens with a Polaroid and a violent action running backward, then tells much of the rest by reverse scene order. Irréversible presents major sections from later to earlier without reversing every shot.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is reverse chronology or a Boomerang . The tell is a normal-speed scene shuffle, or a clip that goes forward then snaps back.
Fix: reverse one recorded action and show fluids, cloth, or debris traveling the wrong way along a single path.

faq.q: What is Reverse Motion in film?
faq.a: Reverse motion is recorded action played backward, so inertia, fluids, and contacts run from effect toward cause inside the shot.

faq.q: Reverse Motion vs Reverse Chronology
faq.a: Reverse motion rewinds the footage. Reverse chronology ( Memento , Irréversible ) reorders ordinary-speed scenes from consequence to cause.

faq.q: When should I use Reverse Motion?
faq.a: When the picture itself must undo physics: rising rain, assembling wreckage, a gesture that should feel like a reversed rite.

faq.q: How do I prompt Reverse Motion for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write time running backward with rain rising and smoke inhaling. Say the clip is reversed. Do not ask for shuffled scene order unless that is the job.
